Country
KūN-trē
n. (rendering Hebrew 'erets and sādeh, Greek chōra and patris)
From Old French contree, from Latin contrata, that which lies over against the beholder — the land spread out before one's eyes. The idea in the root is the land as seen from where a man stands, and so the word carries naturally both the land a man belongs to and the land he is looking toward. Scripture uses it in both directions at once: the country a man is called to leave, and the better country he is travelling to.

Biblical Definition

Country in Scripture is rarely a merely geographical word; it is a word about belonging, and therefore about faith. The life of faith begins with a command to leave one: “Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1). Everything a man's identity rests on — his nation, his clan, his household — is named and surrendered before the promise is even described. The whole of Hebrews 11 then reads that departure as the pattern of all believing: “For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country” (Heb 11:14). The patriarchs died in faith without receiving the promises, and the writer will not let us think they were merely homesick for Mesopotamia — had they been, they had opportunity to return. What they sought was elsewhere: “But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city” (Heb 11:16). Against that stands the far country of the prodigal, the country a man goes to in order to be away from his father: “took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luk 15:13). Two journeys, then, run through Scripture — out of a country toward God, and into a far country away from Him — and every man is on one of them.

Webster 1828 Definition

A tract of land, region, or district; the territory of a nation; the rural parts as distinguished from the town; and the land of one's birth or citizenship, whence the Scripture's better country, which is heavenly.

expand to see more

COUNTRY, n. 1. Properly, the land lying about or near a city; the parts of a region at a distance from a town.

2. A tract of land, or region of indefinite extent; as the hill country, the country of Moab.

3. The kingdom, state or territory in which one is born, or of which one is a citizen; native land.

4. The inhabitants of a region or state taken collectively; as, the whole country rose against him.

5. In Scripture, a better country, that is, an heavenly; the region of the blessed, sought by faith. Heb. 11.

Key Scripture

Genesis 12:1 — "Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:"

Hebrews 11:14 — "For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country."

Hebrews 11:16 — "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city."

Luke 15:13 — "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

Modern Corruption

The heavenly country is emptied of its content and reduced to a metaphor for social improvement here, so that the pilgrim character of the Christian life is lost; or, at the opposite extreme, earthly country is absolutised until patriotism becomes a rival religion.

expand to see more

The first corruption is the quiet deletion of the better country. Where the hope of an actual prepared city is treated as pre-modern imagery for a renewed society in this age, the whole logic of Hebrews 11 collapses: the patriarchs become men who wanted a better Canaan rather than men who confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Scripture will not permit the reduction. God has prepared for them a city — a real one, prepared by a real act, for real persons who died without seeing it. Strip that out and Christian endurance loses its object, and suffering loses its proportion; for it is precisely the weight of the country to come that makes the afflictions of the present time light. A gospel that promises only a better version of here has nothing to say at a graveside.

The opposite corruption absolutises the earthly country. A man's nation is a real gift and a real obligation — Scripture honours the love of one's people, and Paul could wish himself accursed for his kinsmen according to the flesh — but the moment the nation becomes the highest loyalty it becomes an idol, and an idol that has repeatedly demanded blood. The believer holds his citizenship here genuinely and holds it second. Our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour. That ordering does not weaken a man's service to his country; it is the only thing that keeps such service from becoming worship, and the only thing that gives him a standard by which to call his own nation to repentance when it needs it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'erets is land, earth, or country, the commonest word for territory; sādeh is open field or countryside as against the walled town. Greek chōra is a region or district, and patris is the fatherland or native place.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'erets (H776) — earth, land, country; the ordinary word for a territory, as get thee out of thy country (Gen 12:1).

Hebrew sādeh (H7704) — field, open country, the land outside the city wall; rendered country in the men of the country.

Greek chōra (G5561) — region, district, the country as against the city; a far country in Luk 15:13.

Greek patris (G3968) — fatherland, native place; a prophet is not without honour, save in his own country (Mat 13:57).

Greek kreittōn patris epouranios — the better country, that is, an heavenly, of Heb 11:16; the object of patriarchal faith.

Usage

"Of the country to be left at God's call: get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred (Gen 12:1)."

"Of the country sought by faith: they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly (Heb 11:16)."

"Of the far country of the prodigal: took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance (Luk 15:13)."
